newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: South Korean president calls for repentance.
newsitem.headline: South Korean president calls for repentance.

text.p: South Korean President Kim Young-sam, forced to apologise last month over a bribery scandal, on Thursday called on his ruling New Korea Party to repent.
In a display of resolve, he named a strong-willed politician known as "Mr Clean" as new party chairman.
Political analysts said the price Kim would pay in selecting respected former judge Lee Hoi-chang to restore his party's image was the loss of some of his power in the final year of his presidency.
The president now risked becoming a lame duck, they said.
"We as a party should repent and frankly look back at how hard we tried to meet the call of the times by listening to the voice of the people," Kim told a party caucus.
Acknowledging the party faced severe public criticism, he said "people want a humble and responsible attitude from us".
The president apologised on live television last month over a bribes-for-loans scandal involving failed Hanbo Steel Co that snared three of his close aides and his second son.
Lee, 61, is best known for quitting as Kim's prime minister in 1994 to protest curbs on his power. By standing up to Kim he strengthened his reputation of refusing to bend his principles.
"Lee is the most difficult figure for Kim to handle," said Cho Chang-hyun, political science professor at Seoul's Hanyang University.
"To some extent, Kim will have to share power with Lee. He is running out of options and he may be using his last card."
A senior government official who is close to the president said Lee now had a "clear advantage" in a race to become the ruling party torchbearer in presidential elections in December.
Kim is constitutionally barred from seeking a second term.
Lee told the caucus, which unanimously confirmed his nomination, that his pressing task was to ensure a win for his party in the presidential polls.
Lee added to his reputation for integrity by urging the government this week to reopen an investigation into Hanbo, which collapsed with debts of $5.8 billion in January.
Opposition parties have called the probe by state prosecutors a whitewash and are particularly incensed that it exonerated Kim's second son, Kim Hyun-chul.
The senior government official, who asked not to be identified, said Lee faced an uphill task in restoring public faith in the party.
"Although Lee has a great chance to achieve his presidential ambitions, he will also have to go through a very serious test," he said.
Voters this month returned opposition candidates to parliament with landslides in two by-elections in what was seen as a rebuke to the New Korea Party.
"Kim could always dump Lee if he fails to deliver a solution," said one Asian diplomat. "Kim will say: 'I have given you a chance and you blew it'."

Last month, Kim dumped four top presidential Blue House aides as part of a sweeping administration reshuffle designed to restore his credibility. He also changed his prime minister and reshuffled his cabinet.
Another leading contender in the presidential race, Choi Hyung-woo, was felled by a stroke on Tuesday. Choi led Kim loyalists within the ruling camp.
